The proponents of this view have explicitly stated that sale and transfer of ownership in its houses occur only on the building, not on the land, as mentioned by the companions of Abu Hanifah.

(A Note on the Subtlety)

Al-Suhayli said:

He began with "al-ṭā'ifīn" (those who circumambulate) because of their rank and their nearness to the House, the House being the one commanded to be purified for the sake of those who circumambulate. He expressed them with the sound plural (jam' al-salāmah) because the sound plural is more indicative of the verbal root of the act, which is the cause to which the ruling of purification is attached. Had he said "al-ṭawāf" in place of "al-ṭā'ifīn," this word would not have shown the intent of the act as clearly as his saying "lil-ṭā'ifīn." Do you not see that you say "tatūfūn" just as you say "ṭā'ifūn," so the two wordings are alike?

If it is said: Why did he not use the verb itself, which would be clearer, and say: "wa-ṭahhir baytiya lil-ladhīna yaṭūfūn" (And purify My House for those who circumambulate)?

It is answered: The ruling is attached to the act, not to the persons themselves, and the relative "alladhīna" points to the person and the entity, whereas the noun "al-ṭawāf" conceals the meaning of the act rather than clarifying it. So "al-ṭā'ifīn" is more appropriate in this context. Next in rank is "al-qā'imīn" (those who stand), because it has the sense of "al-'ākifīn" (those who remain in devotion), and it has the sense of His saying: ﴿except while you stand over him﴾, meaning persistent and constant. It is like "al-ṭā'ifīn" in the attachment of the ruling of purification to it. Next in rank comes the word "al-rāki'" (those who bow), because those who face the House in bowing are not restricted to those who are near it, as with "al-ṭā'ifīn" and "al-'ākifīn." For this reason the ruling of purification was not attached to this act, which is bowing, and it is not necessary that the one bowing be in the House or near it. Therefore he did not use the sound plural, because it does not need the verb to be clarified as was needed in the earlier words. Then he described "al-rakka'" with "al-sujūd," and did not join them with a conjunction "wa" as he joined what came before, because "al-rukka'" are "al-sujjad" (those who prostrate), and a thing is not joined with "wa" to itself.

There is another benefit: "al-sujūd" most often comes as a verbal noun (maṣdar), and what is meant here is the plural. Had it been joined with "wa," one might have thought it means the sujūd as an act (the maṣdar) rather than the noun which is the adjective.

A third benefit: if the bower does not prostrate, he is not a bower in the ruling of the Sharī'ah. Had it been joined here with "wa," one might have thought that bowing is a ruling that proceeds on its own.

If it is asked: Why did he say "al-sujūd" on the pattern of "fu'ūl" and not "al-sajad" as with "al-rukka'," and in another verse: ﴿rukka'an sujjadan﴾ (bowing, prostrating)? And why was the plural of "sājid" given as "al-sujūd" while the plural of "rāki'" was not given as "rukū'"?

The answer: "al-sujūd" is originally a verbal noun, like "al-khushū'" and "al-khuḍū'," and it encompasses outward and inward prostration. Had he said "al-sajad" as the plural of "sājid," it would encompass only the outward meaning. Likewise "al-rukka'": do you not see that He says: ﴿you see them bowing and prostrating﴾? That is sight of the eye, which relates only to the outward. What is intended here is the outward bowing, since it is joined to what precedes it, which is intended for the purpose of the House, and the House is not faced except by outward action.

As for the humility and submission which the word "rukū'" encompasses but not "rukka'," these are not conditioned on facing the House.

As for "al-sujūd," inasmuch as it indicates the inward meaning, it was made a description of "al-rukka'" and a completion of its meaning, since outward bowing is not valid without inward prostration. And inasmuch as its word also encompasses outward prostration, which is conditioned on facing the House, its arrangement with what precedes it, which is joined to "al-ṭā'ifīn" whom he mentioned by mention of the House, is also fitting.

So whoever attends to these meanings with his heart, and reflects with his intellect upon this wondrous arrangement, rises in knowledge of the inimitability (i'jāz) above mere imitation, and perceives with the eye of certainty that it is a revelation from the All-Wise, the Praiseworthy.

End of his words.

I say: May God have mercy on him, he entered narrow passages through which needles could scarcely pass, and he brought fine points, and other points better than them. As for his explanation of placing Rabī'ah before Mudar, it is in the utmost beauty, for these two names, being mostly associated, became like a single name, so what he mentioned is fine in them.

(Section: On the Secret of the Preference of the Sacred House)

The secret of this preference and distinction has become apparent in the drawing of hearts, the desire and inclination of the hearts, and their love for this secure land. Its pull on hearts is greater than the pull of the magnet on iron, and so it is most fitting for the saying of the poet:

Its beauties are the substance of every beauty, and the magnet of the hearts of men.

For this reason He, glorified is He, informed that it is a "mathābah" for people, meaning they return to it over the passing of years from all regions, and they never have their fill of it; rather, the more they visit it, the more they long for it.

The poet says:
The gaze does not turn away from it when it looks upon it, until the gaze returns to it longing.

So for God, how many slain, despoiled and wounded it has! How much wealth and souls have been expended in its love! The lover has accepted separation from the dearest of his children, his family, his beloved ones and his homeland, sending ahead of himself every kind of fear, loss, hardship and difficulty, yet he delights in all of that and finds it sweet, and if the sovereignty of love appeared in his heart, he would consider it better than the blessings of those who adorn themselves and their luxuries and pleasures.

The poet says:
He is not a lover who counts his misery a torment, when his beloved is pleased.

All of this is the secret of His attributing it to Himself, glorified and exalted is He, by His saying: ﴿And purify My House﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 26]. This special attribution has required of such majesty, glorification and love what it has required, just as His attributing His servant and messenger to Himself required what it required of that, and likewise His attributing His believing servants to Himself clothed them with majesty, love and dignity with which He clothed them. So everything the Lord, exalted is He, attributes to Himself has of superiority and special distinction over others what makes it chosen and selected; then He clothes it, by this attribution, with another preference, specialization and majesty beyond what it had before the attribution. Whoever equated among essences, actions, times and places, and claimed that there is no superiority of any of them over another, and that it is merely preference without a preferrer, has not been granted success in understanding this meaning.

This statement is false for more than forty reasons, which have been mentioned elsewhere.

(Section: From the Signs of Love)

Among them is love for the abode of the beloved and his house, even love for the place where he dwelt. This is the secret for which hearts have been attached to love of the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, so that lovers find it sweet to leave homelands and loved ones to reach it, and the journey, which is a portion of torment, is sweet to them. So they mount dangers, traverse deserts and wastelands, and bear the utmost hardships to reach it, and if it were possible for them they would walk to it upon their eyelids and pupils.

The poet says:
Yes, I would walk to you upon my eyelids, even if the way to your presence is distant.

The secret of this love is the Lord's attributing it to Himself, by His saying: ﴿And purify My House for those who circumambulate﴾.

The poet says:
When you were associated with yourself, you became magnified, and rose in rank above those who were not so associated.

Everything attributed to the beloved is beloved: ﴿And when the servant of God stood calling upon Him﴾; ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night﴾; ﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant﴾; ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant﴾.

Whoever understands this understands the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿In your hand is the good﴾, and the words of His servant and messenger: "At Your service, and at Your bidding; the good is in Your hands, and evil is not attributed to You."

And if one who loves a created being like himself loves its abode, as the poet said:

I pass by the dwellings, the dwelling of Layla; I kiss this wall and that wall.

And:
It was not love of dwellings that enamoured my heart, but love of the one who dwells in them.

Then how about one to whom nothing is like, and whose love is not like any love?

Among the things given precedence in rank: "They will come to you on foot (rijalan), and on every lean camel (kulli dhamir)," because the one who comes on foot comes from a near place, while the one who comes on a lean mount comes from a far place.

It is also narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "I wish I had performed the pilgrimage on foot, because Allah has mentioned those on foot before those riding in the Qur'an."

Ibn Abbas made this an instance of the superior being placed before the less superior. Both meanings exist. Sometimes a thing is placed first for three meanings, four, or five, and sometimes it is placed first for only one of the five.

Consider this parable and how precisely it matches the condition of one who associates partners with Allah and attaches himself to other than Him. In this comparison there are two possible readings:

The first: you may take it as a compound comparison (*tashbih murakkab*), in which the one who associates partners with Allah and worships others alongside Him is likened to a man who has brought about the ruin of his own soul, a ruin from which no salvation can be hoped for. The image is that of one who has fallen from the sky, and the birds have seized him in mid-air and torn him into pieces in their gullets, or the wind has whirled him away and cast him down in some distant place. On this reading, you do not look for a correspondence between each individual element of the thing compared and its counterpart in the thing used for comparison.

The second: it may be a detailed comparison (*tashbih mufarraq*), in which each part of the thing being illustrated is matched with a part of the thing used as the illustration. On this reading, faith and monotheism are likened, in their loftiness, vastness and nobility, to the sky, which is both the place of ascent and the place of descent. From it he descended to the earth, and to it he ascends from it. The one who abandons faith and monotheism is likened to one who has fallen from the sky to the lowest of the low, in terms of severe constriction, accumulated pains, and the birds that snatch his limbs and tear him apart completely, which correspond to the devils that Allah, glorified and exalted is He, sends against him, driving him, goading him, disturbing him and unsettling him toward the places of his destruction. Each devil has a morsel of his religion and heart, just as each bird has a morsel of his flesh and limbs. The wind that hurls him into a remote place is his own desire, which carried him to cast himself into the lowest and farthest place from the sky.

[Section: The Station of Magnifying the Sacred Limits of Allah]

Among the stations of "*You alone do we worship, and You alone do we ask for help*" (﴿إيّاكَ نَعْبُدُ وإيّاكَ نَسْتَعِينُ﴾) is the station (*manzila*) of magnifying the sacred limits of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And whoever magnifies the sacred limits of Allah, it is better for him with his Lord﴾ [al-Hajj: 30].

A group of the exegetes said: "The sacred limits of Allah here are the things that provoke His anger and what He has forbidden, and magnifying them is abstaining from engaging with them." Al-Layth said: "The sacred limits of Allah are that which is not permissible to violate." Others said: "The limits are the commands and prohibitions." Al-Zajjaj said: "A *hurma* (sacred limit) is that which it is obligatory to uphold and forbidden to neglect." Others said: "The sacred limits here are the rites (*manasik*) and the sacred places and times of the Hajj."

The correct view is that the sacred limits encompass all of this. They are the plural of *hurma*, which is that which must be respected and preserved, whether rights, persons, times or places. Magnifying them means giving each its due and guarding it from being wasted.

The author of *al-Manazil* said:

"*Al-hurma* is *al-tahharruj* (scrupulous avoidance) of violations and of audacious transgressions."

*Al-tahharruj* means emerging from the constriction (*haraj*) of violation. The pattern *tafa''ala* (as in *tahharraja*) can indicate entering into something, as in *tamanna* (to wish, i.e. to enter into desire) when one enters into a wish, or *tawallaja fi al-amr* (to enter deeply into a matter), meaning he went into it. It can also indicate leaving it, as in *takharraja*, *tahawwab* and *ta'atham*, when one wishes to exit from *haraj* (constriction). *Al-hub* means sin (*ithm*).

He meant that *al-hurma* is the emerging from the constriction of violation and from the boldness of daring to commit it. Since the one who violates is of two kinds, the bold and the timid, he said: "*from violations and audacious transgressions*."

The strongest cause for rejecting testimony, legal opinion (*futya*) and transmission (*riwaya*) is lying, because it is a corruption in the very instrument of testimony, legal opinion and transmission. For this reason Allah, glorified is He, makes the emblem of the one who lies about Him on the Day of Resurrection, and the emblem of the one who lies about His Messenger, to be the blackness of their faces. Lying has a great effect on the blackening of the face, and it covers it with a veil of hatred that every truthful person sees. The mark of the liar is proclaimed upon his face to whoever has two eyes. The truthful, Allah grants him reverence and dignity, so whoever sees him is in awe of him and loves him. Consider this parable and how precisely it matches the condition of one who associates partners with Allah and attaches himself to other than Him. In this comparison there are two possible readings:

The first: you may take it as a compound comparison (*tashbih murakkab*), in which the one who associates partners with Allah and worships others alongside Him is likened to a man who has brought about the ruin of his own soul, a ruin from which no salvation can be hoped for. The image is that of one who has fallen from the sky, and the birds have seized him in mid-air and torn him into pieces in their gullets, or the wind has whirled him away and cast him down in some distant place. On this reading, you do not look for a correspondence between each individual element of the thing compared and its counterpart in the thing used for comparison.

The second: it may be a detailed comparison (*tashbih mufarraq*), in which each part of the thing being illustrated is matched with a part of the thing used as the illustration. On this reading, faith and monotheism are likened, in their loftiness, vastness and nobility, to the sky, which is both the place of ascent and the place of descent. From it he descended to the earth, and to it he ascends from it. The one who abandons faith and monotheism is likened to one who has fallen from the sky to the lowest of the low, in terms of severe constriction, accumulated pains, and the birds that snatch his limbs and tear him apart completely, which correspond to the devils that Allah, glorified and exalted is He, sends against him, driving him, goading him, disturbing him and unsettling him toward the places of his destruction. Each devil has a morsel of his religion and heart, just as each bird has a morsel of his flesh and limbs. The wind that hurls him into a remote place is his own desire, which carried him to cast himself into the lowest and farthest place from the sky.

Abu al-Darda, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "How excellent is the sleep of the intelligent and their breaking of the fast, and how they are cheated by it: the standing in prayer of fools and their fasting. And a grain of mustard seed from one possessing taqwa is better than mountains of worship from the self-deceived." This is among the jewels of speech and one of the clearest proofs of the perfect understanding of the Companions and their precedence over those after them in every good, may Allah be pleased with them all.

Know, then, that the servant only traverses the stages of the journey to Allah with his heart and his resolve, not with his body alone. Taqwa in reality is taqwa of the hearts, not taqwa of the limbs. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And whoever honours the symbols of Allah, indeed it is from the taqwa of the hearts﴾.

And He said: ﴿It is not their flesh nor their blood that reaches Allah, but taqwa from you reaches Him﴾.

And the Prophet ﷺ said: "Taqwa is here," and he pointed to his chest.

So the intelligent person covers in distance, through soundness of determination, loftiness of aspiration, singleness of intention, and sincerity of purpose, with little action, many times over what the idle person covers with much exertion and arduous travel. For determination and love dispel hardship and make the journey pleasant. Advancement and precedence toward Allah, glorified is He, are only by aspirations and sincerity of desire and determination. Thus the one of high aspiration advances, while remaining still, over the one of much action by stages. If he equals him in aspiration, the other is ahead of him through his action. This is a matter that requires detailed explanation, in which Islam and ihsan agree.

The most complete guidance is the guidance of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who gave each of the two their due. With his perfection, his will, and his states with Allah, he would stand in prayer until his feet swelled, fast until it was said he never breaks his fast, strive in the way of Allah, mix with his Companions without withdrawing from them, and not abandon any supererogatory acts or litanies because of those divine visitations which the powers of humans cannot bear.

Allah the Exalted commanded His servants to uphold the laws of Islam in their outward forms and the realities of faith in their inward hearts, and He accepts neither of them without its companion and partner.

In the Musnad, it is related in a marfu' report: "Islam is outward, and faith is in the heart." So every outward Islam that does not lead its possessor to the inner reality of faith does not benefit him until there is some inner faith with it. And every inner reality whose possessor does not uphold the outward laws of Islam does not benefit, however great it may be. Even if the heart is torn apart by love and fear, but he does not worship by the command and the apparent Shari'ah, that will not save him from the Fire, just as if he upholds the outward forms of Islam while there is not the reality of faith within him, that will not save him from the Fire.

When this is understood, the truthful travellers to Allah and the Last Abode are of two types. One type directs whatever remains of their time after the obligations to bodily supererogatory acts and makes them their habit, without being eager to realize the works of the hearts, their stations, and their rulings, though they are not devoid of its root. Rather, their aspirations are directed toward increasing actions. The other type directs whatever remains after the obligations and the sunnah to caring for the soundness of their hearts, their devotion to Allah alone, their collectedness toward Him, and guarding their thoughts and volitions with Him. They make this the strength of their worship through the works of the hearts: correcting love, fear, hope, reliance, and turning in repentance. They see that the slightest share of divine visitations that descend upon their hearts from Allah is dearer to them than many bodily voluntary acts. So when one of them attains collectedness, a visitation of intimacy, love, longing, or brokenness and humility, he does not exchange it for anything else at all, unless a command comes, in which case he hastens to it with that visitation if he is able, and if not, he hastens to the command even though the visitation departs. When supererogatory acts come, here is the arena of hesitation. If he can perform them with that state, well and good. Otherwise, he considers which is weightier and more beloved to Allah: is it to perform that supererogatory act, even if its visitation departs, such as relieving the distressed, guiding the lost, mending the broken, gaining faith for someone, and the like? Here it is proper to prefer the weightier supererogatory act. Whenever he prefers these out of desire for Allah and seeking nearness to Him, Allah will return to him what he missed of the visitation, stronger than it was at another time. If the visitation is weightier than the supererogatory act, then the prudent course is to persist in the visitation until it withdraws from him, for it will be lost, whereas the supererogatory act is not lost. This is a matter that requires abundant understanding of the path, the ranks of actions, and giving priority to the more important among them. And Allah is the One who grants success in that; there is no god but Him, and no lord besides Him.

Mujahid said: "It regrets what has passed and says: 'If only I had done it! If only I had not done it!'"

Al-Farra' said: "There is no soul, righteous or wicked, except that it blames itself: if it has done good, it says: 'Why did I not do more?' and if it has done evil, it says: 'I wish I had not done it.'"

So the difficulty of the ascent and the sitting of that frightener at its summit come together, along with the weakness of the traveler's resolve and intention. At that point the journey becomes easy, the obstacles of the road disappear from him, and the hardship of its obstacles vanishes, and he sees a wide, safe road that leads him to the stations and the watering places. On it are the signposts, and in it are the resting places, prepared for the caravan of the Most Merciful.

So between the servant and happiness and success lies: strength of resolve, an hour of patience, boldness of soul, and steadfastness of heart.

Grace is in the hand of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills. And Allah is the Possessor of great grace.

(Section)

and he sees his preoccupation with that and his attention to it as a descent from his station, a sinking from his rank, and a return upon his heels.

If it overtakes him without his solicitation or choice, then let him treat it by witnessing the favour (of God), by fear of (God's) scheming, and by his not knowing the end upon which he will be found (at death).

And God is the One sought for help.

If it overtakes him without his solicitation or choice, then let him treat it by witnessing the favour (of God), by fear of (God's) scheming, and by his not knowing the end upon which he will be found (at death).

And God is the One sought for help.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 22, verse 38:

He, glorified and exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah defends those who have believed﴾. In another reading it is: ﴿Indeed, Allah repels﴾.

So His repelling and His defending on their behalf is in proportion to the strength of their faith and its perfection.

The root of faith and its strength lies in the remembrance of Allah, the Exalted. Whoever has a more perfect faith and remembers Allah more often, Allah's repelling and defending on his behalf is greater. Whoever falls short, it falls short accordingly: remembrance for remembrance, and forgetfulness for forgetfulness.

And he said in (Tariq al-Hijratayn, "The Path of the Two Migrations"):

The perfection of repelling and defending is in proportion to the strength and weakness of faith. When the soul becomes free, good, at peace, and rich with what its Owner and Originator (Fatir) has made it rich with, namely the light that falls into the heart and overflows from it to the soul, then through that richness it stays steadfast upon the bestowed matter, is safe thereby from the displeasing matter, and is cleared of showing off (riya'). The pivot of all of this is steadfastness, inwardly and outwardly. For this reason the whole of religion is in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So be steadfast as you have been commanded﴾ [Hud: 112], and He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then are steadfast, there will be no fear concerning them, nor will they grieve﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 13].

[Section: On the Permission to Fight]

When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ settled in Medina, and Allah strengthened him with the support of His believing servants, the Helpers (al-Ansar), and joined their hearts together after the enmity and resentments that had existed between them, the Helpers of Allah and the battalion of Islam protected him against the black and the red alike. They offered their lives in his defense and preferred their love for him over their love for their fathers, their sons, and their wives, and he was more deserving of them than their own selves. The Arabs and the Jews shot at them from one bow, rolled up their sleeves for enmity and war, and cried out against them from every side. Allah, glorified is He, commanded them to be patient, to pardon, and to overlook, until their strength grew firm and their wing became powerful. Then He permitted them to fight at that time, without making it obligatory upon them. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged. And indeed, Allah is competent to give them victory﴾ [al-Hajj: 39].

Some have said that this permission was given in Mecca and that the surah is Meccan. This is an error, for several reasons:

First: Allah did not grant them permission to fight in Mecca, nor did they have the strength by which they could carry out fighting in Mecca.

Second: The context of the verse indicates that the permission came after the Hijrah (emigration) and their expulsion from their homes, for He says: ﴿who have been expelled from their homes without right, only because they say, "Our Lord is Allah"﴾ [al-Hajj: 40], and these are the Emigrants (al-Muhajirun).

Third: His saying, ﴿These two adversaries dispute concerning their Lord﴾ [al-Hajj: 19], was revealed concerning those from both groups who fought in single combat on the day of Badr.

Fourth: At its end He addressed them with His saying: ﴿O you who have believed﴾ [al-Hajj: 77].

All of this address is Medinan. As for the address ﴿O mankind﴾, it is common to both.

Fifth: In it He commanded jihad that encompasses jihad by the hand and other than it. There is no doubt that the command to general jihad came only after the Hijrah. As for the jihad of argument (jihad al-hujjah), He commanded it in Mecca with His saying: ﴿So do not obey the disbelievers, and strive against them with it﴾ [al-Furqan: 52], meaning with the Qur'an, ﴿a great jihad﴾.

So this surah is Meccan, and the jihad in it is the conveying of the message and the jihad of argument. As for the jihad commanded in Surat al-Hajj, it includes jihad by the sword.

Sixth: Al-Hakim narrated in his "al-Mustadrak," from the hadith of al-A'mash, from Muslim al-Batin, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ left Mecca, Abu Bakr said: "They have expelled their Prophet! Indeed we belong to Allah and to Him we return! They will surely perish." Then Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed: ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged﴾ [al-Hajj: 39].

This is the first verse revealed concerning fighting.

Its chain of narration meets the conditions of the "Two Sahihs" (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim). The context of the surah indicates that it contains both Meccan and Medinan material, for the story of Satan's casting into the recitation of the Messenger (the "Gharaniq" incident) is Meccan. And Allah knows best.

[Section: On the Divisions of Jihad]

When the contest was legislated so that the believer may learn fighting, become accustomed to it, and train in it, it is known that the fighter may intend to repel the enemy when the fighter is the one being pursued and the enemy is the pursuer. He may also intend to gain victory over the enemy from the outset when he is the pursuer and the enemy is the one pursued. He may also intend both matters. The categories are three, and the believer is commanded to engage in jihad in each of them.

Jihad of repulsion (jihad al-daf') is more difficult than jihad of pursuit (jihad al-talab), for jihad of repulsion resembles the rule of repelling an aggressor (al-sa'il), and for this reason it is permitted for the wronged person to defend himself,

as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged﴾.

The Prophet ﷺ also said: "Whoever is killed defending his property is a martyr, and whoever is killed defending his blood is a martyr." Repelling an aggressor on account of religion is jihad and an act of devotion, while repelling an aggressor on account of property and self is permissible and a concession. If one is killed in that, he is a martyr.

Thus fighting in repulsion is broader than fighting in pursuit and more general in its obligation. For this reason it becomes obligatory upon every person who is present and fights in it: the slave with or without his master's permission, the son without his parents' permission, and the debtor without his creditor's permission. This is like the jihad of the Muslims on the day of Uhud and the Trench (al-Khandaq).

It is not a condition in this type of jihad that the enemy be no more than twice the number of the Muslims or fewer, for on the day of Uhud and the Trench they were many times the number of the Muslims, and jihad was obligatory upon them, because at that time it was jihad of necessity and repulsion, not jihad of choice. For this reason the prayer of fear (salat al-khawf) is permitted in this type according to the circumstances.

Is it permitted in jihad of pursuit if one fears that the enemy will escape but does not fear their return?

On this there are two opinions among the scholars, which are two narrations from Imam Ahmad.

It is known that the jihad in which a person is both pursuer and pursued is more obligatory than this jihad in which he is a pursuer and not pursued. And souls are more eager for it than for both of these.

As for pure jihad of pursuit, none desires it except one of two men: either one of great faith who fights so that the word of Allah may be supreme and the religion may be entirely for Allah, or one who desires booty and captives.

Jihad of repulsion is intended by everyone, and no one turns away from it except the coward, who is blameworthy by both law and reason. Pure jihad of pursuit for the sake of Allah is intended by the lords of the believers. As for the jihad in which one is both pursuer and pursued, it is intended by the best of people for the elevation of the word of Allah and His religion, and it is intended by the average of them for repulsion and for love of victory.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 22, verse 40:

Al-Zajjaj said: "The interpretation of this is: Were it not for Allah's repelling people, some of them by means of others, there would have been demolished—in the sharia of every prophet—the place in which prayer is performed. So, were it not for the repelling, there would have been demolished in the time of Musa the churches in which he used to pray under his sharia, and in the time of Isa the hermitages (ṣawāmiʿ) and churches (biyaʿ), and in the time of Muhammad (ﷺ) the mosques."

Al-Azhari said: "Allah, glorified is He, informed that, were it not for His repelling some people from corruption by means of others, there would have been demolished the places of worship of every group of the people of His religion and obedience at every time. He began with mentioning the ṣawāmiʿ and biya', because the prayers of the earlier prophets of the Children of Israel and their companions were in them before the revelation of the Qur'an, and the mosques were placed later because they came into being after them."

Ibn Zayd said: "The ṣalawat are the prayers of the people of Islam, which are cut off when the enemy enters upon them."

Al-Akhfash said: "According to this view, the ṣalawat are not demolished, but they take the place of another act, as if he had said: 'Prayers were abandoned.'"

Abu ʿUbayda said: "It means the places of prayer."

Al-Hasan said: "The places of prayer of the people of the dhimma are repelled by means of the believers."

According to this view, there is no need for the supposition that those who held the first view made, and this is the apparent meaning of the wording, with no difficulty in it in any way. The verse indicates what has actually occurred; it does not indicate that these places—other than the mosques—are beloved and pleasing to Him. Rather, He informed that, were it not for His repelling people, some by means of others, there would have been demolished these places which were beloved to Him before Islam, and He kept in existence what He kept after it, even if they were hateful to Him, just as He kept the people of the dhimma, even though He hates them and abhors them, and repels from them by means of the Muslims despite His hatred for them.

Likewise He repels from the places of their worship by means of the Muslims even if He hates them. He, glorified is He, repels from their places of worship, which they were kept in both by sharia and by decree. So He loves the repelling from them even though He hates them, just as He loves the repelling from their adherents even though He hates them.

This view is the strongest, Allah willing, and it is the position of Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim said in his "Tafsir": Abu Saʿid al-Ashajj narrated to us: ʿUbayd Allah—he is Ibn Musa—narrated to us from Israʾil, from al-Suddi, from one who narrated to him from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: ﴿Had there been demolished hermitages and churches﴾

He said: The ṣawāmiʿ are those in which the monks reside, the biya' are the synagogues of the Jews, the ṣalawat are the churches of the Christians, and the masajid are the mosques of the Muslims.

Ibn Abi Hatim said: And al-Ashajj informed us: Hafs ibn Ghiyath narrated to us, from Dawud, from Abu al-ʿAliya, who said: ﴿Had there been demolished hermitages﴾

He said: Hermitages, even if there is associating partners with Him! And in another wording: Indeed Allah loves to be remembered, even by a disbeliever.

In the tafsir of Shayban, from Qatada: The ṣawāmiʿ are for the Sabians, the biya' for the Christians, the ṣalawat for the Jews, and the masajid for the Muslims.

The verse has included mention of the monastery (dayr), the cell (qilaya), the church (kanisa), and the hermitage (ṣawma'a).

As for the dayr, it is specific to the Christians; they build it for the monks outside the town, where they gather for monasticism and withdrawal from people.

As for the qilaya, their monks build it elevated like a minaret. The difference between it and the dayr is that they gather in the dayr, whereas the qilaya is only for one person who isolates himself; it has no door, but rather has an opening from which he takes his food, drink, and whatever he needs.

As for the ṣawma'a, it is like the qilaya, belonging to the monk alone.

Al-Azhari said: The ṣawma'a among buildings was named ṣawma'a because its top is slender. It is said: ṣamaʿa al-tharida, when he raised its head and sharpened it, and a thariddah is called ṣawma'a when it is like that; and from this it is said: "a man with a ṣa'mad heart" when he is sharp in intelligence.

Some made a distinction between the ṣawma'a and the qilaya: that the qilaya is situated isolated in a desert of the land, while the ṣawma'a is on the roads.

As for the biya', it is the plural of bi'a, and the people of language and tafsir agree that it is the place of worship of the Christians, except what we related from Ibn ʿAbbas, that he said: "The biya' are the mosques of the Jews."

As for the kanaʾis, it is the plural of kanisa, and it belongs to the People of the Book; and specifically for the Jews, the fuhur—with the fa' and ha' vowelled—whose singular is fuhr, which is the house of study (midras) in which they study knowledge together.

In a hadith: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered upon the Jews in their house of study (bayt midrasihim)."

And in it also is the saying of Anas: "It was as if they were the Jews when they came out of their fuhr."

The ruling for all these places is the ruling of the church. It is necessary to draw attention to this.

As for the seeing of the heart: it is the unveiling of the form of the known object to it, such that its relation to the heart is like the relation of the visible to the eye. Allah, glorified is He, made the heart see and become blind, just as the eye sees and becomes blind. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿For indeed, it is not the eyes that go blind, but it is the hearts within the breasts that go blind﴾.

So the heart sees and hears, and it goes blind and deaf. Its blindness and deafness are more severe than the blindness and deafness of sight.

This is the question on which the jurists differed: is the intellect (al-'aql) in the heart or in the brain? There are two opinions, reported as two narrations from Imam Ahmad.

The verified position is that its origin and substance are from the heart, and it terminates in the brain. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Have they not travelled through the land, so that they have hearts with which to understand (ya'qilūna) or ears with which to hear?﴾

So He made the intellect in the heart, just as He made hearing through the ear and sight through the eye. He, the Exalted, also said: ﴿Indeed, in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart (qalb)﴾.

More than one of the early generations (al-salaf) said: "for whoever has intellect ('aql)."

Others argued that a man may be struck on the head and his intellect is lost, and that if the intellect were not in the head it would not have been lost. For hearing and sight are not lost by a blow to the hand or the foot, nor to any other limb, since they are not connected to these.

The proponents of the heart replied that its loss through corruption of the brain does not preclude that it is in the heart, because of the connection between the heart and the head. This is like how the growth of beard hair does not preclude the removal of the two testicles, and how the corruption of a faculty may happen through the corruption of the organ, because the organ is its locus and is connected to it. And Allah knows best.

In any case, that is among the greatest of Allah's signs, proofs, power and wisdom: how the image of the heavens and the earth, the seas, the sun, the moon, the regions, the kingdoms and the nations can be imprinted in this small place. A person memorizes very many books, various and numerous sciences, and different crafts, and all of them are imprinted in this small part, without some of these images mixing with others. Rather, each image is by itself fixed in this locus. If you were to try to carve many images and shapes into a small place, some would mix with others and some would obliterate others. Yet in this small part many different and even opposing images are inscribed, and none of them nullifies another.

Among the most wondrous things is that this intellectual faculty receives what the senses convey to it, so they gather in it, and then each sense restores the benefit of the other sense. For example, you see a person and know that he is so-and-so; you hear his voice and know that it is him; you touch a thing and recognize it; you smell it and know that it is it. Then you infer from what you hear of his voice that he is the one you saw, so hearing his voice suffices you in place of seeing him and stands in for witnessing him. For this reason most jurists permitted the testimony of a blind man, and his buying and selling, and they agreed on the permissibility of his having intercourse with his wife, even though he has never seen her, relying on her voice. Indeed, even if she were mute and he were deaf, it would still be permissible for him to have intercourse with her.

Allah, glorified is He, has placed between hearing, sight and the heart (fu'ād) a connection, linkage and interpenetration by which one of them stands in for another. For this reason He often mentions them together in His Book, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the hearing, the sight and the heart, all of those will be questioned about﴾, and His saying: ﴿And We made for them hearing, sight and hearts (af'ida)﴾, and His saying: ﴿They have hearts with which they do not understand, and they have eyes with which they do not see, and they have ears with which they do not hear﴾. This is from the Creator's care, glorified is He, for the perfection of this human form, so that each sense stands in for the other and performs its function in general, though not in everything.

Then He, the Exalted, deposited in him the faculty of reflection (tafakkur) and commanded him to use it in what benefits him in this world and the Hereafter. He composed the reflective faculty from two of the present things that are at hand to the retentive faculty, in a particular composition. From between these two things a third, new thing arises, of which the intellect had no awareness, though its materials were with it. But through the composition, the third matter came about for it. From here arose the extraction of crafts, trades and sciences, the building of cities and dwellings, and matters of agriculture and farming, and other things. When the reflective faculty extracts this and approves of it, it hands it over to the volitional, cognitive faculty, which transfers it from the register of minds to the register of existing things. Thus it was a mental matter and then became an external existing reality. Had it not been for reflection, a person would not have been guided to attain benefits and ward off harms. This is among the greatest blessings and the completion of divine care. For this reason, when animals, the insane and the like lack this faculty, they are unable to attain what those endowed with thought attain.

Since extracting the sought matter by this way involves thinking and measuring, one thinks first in extracting the material, then measures it and sets it out second, as a tailor produces a garment and then measures and cuts it. He, the Exalted, said concerning [al-Walīd]: ﴿Leave Me with the one whom I created alone, and to whom I granted abundant wealth, and sons present with him, and smoothed for him (all) smoothing. Then he desires that I should add more. No! Indeed, he has been stubborn toward Our signs. I will overwhelm him with a steep ascent. Indeed, he reflected and calculated, so may he be destroyed, how he calculated! Then may he be destroyed, how he calculated!﴾

So He repeated "calculated" (qaddara) without "reflected" (fakkara), and condemned him for it without the other. This is set according to the requirement of the situation, for by reflection he sought to extract the unknown, and that is not blameworthy. But once he extracted it, he made two judgments: a general judgment and a particular judgment.

The general judgment is that the sorcerer is the one who separates a man from his wife.

The particular judgment is that the one who separates a man from his wife is blameworthy. So here there is one judgment after another, and for this He repeated it and condemned him for it.

As for reflection, it is the seeking of knowledge of a thing, so it is not blamed. This is unlike one who, after his reflection, calculates what leads him to establish falsehood and nullify truth. So reflect upon it.

[Section: Sins Blind the Insight]

Among their punishments is that they blind the insight of the heart, extinguish its light, block the paths of knowledge, and veil the sources of guidance.

Malik said to al-Shafi'i when he met him and saw those signs: "I see that Allah, the Exalted, has cast a light upon your heart, so do not extinguish it with the darkness of disobedience."

This light continues to weaken and fade, while the darkness of disobedience grows stronger until the heart becomes like a pitch-black night. How many a person falls into ruin in it without seeing, like a blind man who goes out at night on a road full of perils and destruction. How precious is safety, and how swift is ruin! Then those darknesses grow stronger and overflow from the heart to the limbs, so blackness covers the face according to their strength and increase. When death comes, they appear in the barzakh (intermediate realm), and the grave fills with darkness, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed these graves are filled with darkness for their occupants, and indeed Allah illuminates them for them through my prayer upon them."

When the Day of Return comes and the servants are gathered, the darkness rises over the faces, a manifest rising that everyone sees, until the face becomes black like a burnt coal. How grievous a punishment, which cannot be weighed against all the pleasures of this world from beginning to end! How then about the portion of a servant who is troubled, distressed and weary, in a time that is but an hour of a dream? And Allah is the One sought for help.

(Section heading)

**[Section]**

As for His words, ﴿that He may make what Satan throws in a trial for those in whose hearts is a disease, and the hard-hearted﴾, the particle here retains its original sense: it is the *lam* of wisdom and causation (*lam al-hikmah wa'l-ta'lil*). God, glorified is He, informs us that He made what Satan had cast into the wish of the Messenger a test and a trial for His servants. Two groups were thereby put to trial: those in whose hearts is a disease, and those whose hearts are hard. He also made the believers know that the Qur'an and the Messenger are true, and that Satan's casting is false. So they believed in this, and their hearts became humbly submissive to it. This is a sought-after and intended end through this divine decree and measure.

God, glorified is He, made hearts into three categories: diseased, hard, and humbly submissive (*mukhbitah*). This is because a heart is either dry and rigid, not softening to the truth in acknowledgment and submission, or it is not like that. The first is the state of hard, stony hearts that do not accept what is instilled in them, in which the truth is not impressed and beneficial knowledge is not engraved, and which do not soften to the performance of righteous deeds. As for the second type, it is either that the truth is firmly established in it and does not depart from it, because of its strength together with its softness, or that it is established with weakness and dissolution. The second is the diseased heart, and the first is the sound, humbly submissive heart. It combines firmness, purity, and softness: it sees the truth through its purity, is strengthened in it through its firmness, and shows mercy to creatures through its softness. As in a transmitted report: "The hearts are the vessels of God on His earth, so the most beloved of them to God are the firmest, the softest and the purest."

As God, the Exalted, said of the people of these hearts: ﴿Hard against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves﴾ (48:29).

This is a description by Him of the believers who recognized faith through the purity of their hearts, were firm against the disbelievers through their hardness, and showed mercy among themselves through their softness. This is because the heart is one of the organs of the body. It is the noblest of its organs and its obeyed sovereign. Every organ, such as the hand for instance, is either rigid and dry, not bending and not gripping, or it grips weakly, and this is like the hard heart. Or it is diseased, weak, and incapable, and due to its weakness and disease, this is like the one who has a disease. Or it is gripping with strength and softness, and this is like the knowing, merciful heart. Through knowledge it has come out of the disease arising from desire and doubt, and through mercy it has come out of hardness. For this reason God, glorified is He, described those other than the owners of the diseased and hard hearts by knowledge, faith, and humble submission. So reflect on the manifestation of His wisdom, glorified is He, in the owners of these hearts, who are the whole community. He informed us that those given knowledge know that it is the truth from their Lord, just as He informed us that they say, regarding the ambiguous (*mutashabih*) verses, "We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord." Both attributes are subject to doubt. So their portion of it was faith, and the portion of the owners of hearts deviating from soundness was trial. For this reason God, glorified is He, made the firm (*ihkam*) rulings of His verses correspond to what Satan casts. The firm verses correspond to the ambiguous ones. So the making firm here is like the sending down of the firm verses there, and the abrogation (*naskh*) of what Satan casts here corresponds to the referral of the ambiguous to the firm there. Abrogation here means lifting what Satan cast, not lifting what the Lord, glorified is He, legislated. Abrogation has another meaning as well: abrogating from the understanding of the addressees what they understood from it that was not intended, and that the wording did not indicate, even if it gave that impression. Just as the Companions applied the term "abrogation" to His words: ﴿Whether you show what is in your souls or conceal it, God will call you to account for it, then He forgives whom He wills﴾ (2:284). They said: "It was abrogated by His words: ﴿Our Lord, do not take us to task if we forget or err﴾ (2:286), and the rest of the verse."

This is abrogation of understanding, not abrogation of an established ruling, since being called to account does not necessarily entail punishment, either in the Hereafter or in this world. For this reason He made the call to account general to them all, then afterwards informed that He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills. So understanding from the verse the taking to task, which is punishment, is loading it beyond its capacity. Therefore this meaning was lifted from their understanding by His words: ﴿Our Lord, do not take us to task if we forget or err﴾, to the end of it.

This is the lifting of an understanding of something other than the intended meaning of what the angel cast, and that is the lifting of what someone other than the angel cast into their hearing or into the wish. Abrogation has a third meaning according to the Companions and the Successors (*tabi'un*): leaving the apparent meaning, either by specifying a general ruling or by restricting an absolute one. This is very frequent in their speech. It has a fourth meaning, which later scholars know and on which they have agreed: lifting a ruling entirely after its establishment by a lifting proof. So these are four meanings of abrogation, and making firm has three meanings.

The first is making firm that corresponds to the ambiguous, as in His words: ﴿He it is who sent down to you the Book, in it are firm verses, which are the mother of the Book, and others ambiguous﴾ (3:7).

The second is making firm that corresponds to the abrogation of what Satan casts, as in His words: ﴿Then God abrogates what Satan casts, then God makes His verses firm﴾ (22:52). This making firm encompasses all His verses: it is their establishment, confirmation, and clarification. Among its uses is His words: ﴿A Book whose verses are made firm﴾ (11:1).

The third is making firm that corresponds to the abrogated verses, as the early generations often say: "This verse is firm and not abrogated." This is because making firm sometimes occurs in the revelation, and then it corresponds to what Satan casts in his wish, whether what the transmitter casts or what enters the transmitter's hearing. The ruling here is what God sent down. God made it firm, that is, He distinguished it from its confusion with what was not sent down, and He separated from it what is not from it by invalidating it. Sometimes it occurs in preserving the revealed text and its continuance, so it is not abrogated after its establishment. And sometimes it occurs in the meaning of the revealed text and its interpretation, which is distinguishing the intended meaning from other meanings so that it is not confused with them.

The point is that His words ﴿so that He may make what Satan casts a trial for those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ have the *lam* of causation in its original sense. This test and trial manifest the three different hearts. The hard and diseased hearts have had their concealed doubt and disbelief exposed. The humbly submissive heart has had its concealed faith and guidance exposed, along with increased love for it and increased hatred of disbelief and polytheism and aversion from them. This is among the greatest wisdoms of this casting.

**[Section: The difference between the angel's inspiration and Satan's casting]**

The difference between the inspiration of the angel and the casting of Satan is in several respects:

Among them: whatever is pleasing to God and in accordance with what His Messenger brought is from the angel, and whatever is for other than Him and not pleasing to Him is from Satan's casting.

Among them: whatever produces turning to God, repentance to Him, remembrance of Him, and an ascending aspiration toward Him is from the angel's casting, and whatever produces the opposite is from Satan's casting.

Among them: whatever produces intimacy, light in the heart, and expansion of the chest is from the angel, and whatever produces the opposite is from Satan.

Among them: whatever produces tranquility and calm is from the angel, and whatever produces anxiety, agitation, and turmoil is from Satan.

The angelic inspiration is frequent in pure, clean hearts that have been illuminated by God's light. The angel has a connection with them and an affinity between him and them, for he is good and pure and only approaches a heart that suits him. So the angel's whisper into this heart is more frequent than Satan's whisper. As for a dark heart that has blackened with the smoke of desires and doubts, Satan's casting and whispering into it are more frequent than the angel's whisper.

**[Section: On the division of hearts into sound, sick, and dead]**

Since the heart is described as living or its opposite, it is divided according to this into these three states.

The sound heart is the sound (*salim*) heart, which none will be saved on the Day of Resurrection except one who comes to God with it, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿The Day when neither wealth nor children will benefit, except one who comes to God with a sound heart﴾ (26:88–89).

The word *salim* is "sound," and it follows this pattern because it denotes attributes, like *tawil* (long), *qasir* (short), and *zarif* (witty). So the sound heart is one in which soundness has become a stable attribute, like *alim* (knowing) and *qadir* (capable). Also, it is the opposite of the diseased, the sick, and the ailing.

People's expressions differ regarding the meaning of the sound heart. The comprehensive matter about it is that it is the one that has been freed from every desire that contradicts God's command and prohibition, and from every doubt that opposes His report. It is free from servitude to anything other than Him, and free from judging by other than His Messenger. It is free in loving anything alongside God, and from fearing, hoping in, relying upon, turning to, humbling itself to, and preferring the pleasure of others over His pleasure in every circumstance, and it keeps far from His wrath by every means. This is the reality of servitude that is only fit for God alone.

So the sound heart is the one free from any polytheism toward other than God in any way. Rather, its servitude is purely for God, the Exalted: in intention, love, reliance, turning, humble submission, fear, and hope. Its deeds are purely for God. If it loves, it loves for God's sake; if it hates, it hates for God's sake; if it gives, it gives for God; if it withholds, it withholds for God. And this is not sufficient for it until it is free from submission and judging by anyone other than the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It firmly ties its heart to him, in following and imitating him alone, above anyone else, in statements and deeds. These are the statements of the heart, which are beliefs; and the statements of the tongue, which are reports of what is in the heart; and the deeds of the heart, which are intention, love, dislike, and their consequences; and the deeds of the limbs.

The judge over all of this, in its smallest and greatest matters, is what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) brought. It does not advance ahead of him with any belief, statement, or deed, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿O you who believe, do not put yourselves forward before God and His Messenger﴾ (49:1).

That is, do not speak until he speaks, and do not act until he commands. One of the early generations said: "No act, however small, is without two registers being opened for it: why? and how?" That is, why did you do it, and how did you do it? The first is a question about the cause of the act, its motive, and its driver: is it an immediate personal benefit of the doer, a worldly aim such as love of praise from people or fear of their blame, or attracting something desired immediately, or repelling something disliked immediately? Or is the motive of the act fulfilling the rights of servitude and seeking closeness and affection toward the Lord, glorified is He, and seeking a means to Him?

The place of this question is: were you obliged to do this act for your Master, or did you do it for your own desire and whim?

The second is a question about following the Messenger, peace be upon him, in that worship: was that deed something I legislated for you through my Messenger, or was it a deed I did not legislate and did not approve?

The first is a question about sincerity, and the second about following. God, glorified is He, accepts no deed except with both.

The way to be freed from the first question is by purifying sincerity, and the way to be freed from the second question is by achieving following. The sound heart is free from an intention that contradicts sincerity, and from a desire that contradicts following. This is the reality of the sound heart, to which salvation and happiness are guaranteed.

**[Section on the dead heart]**

The second heart is the opposite of this: the dead heart, with no life in it. It does not know its Lord, and does not worship Him by His command or by what He loves and approves. Rather, it stands with its desires and pleasures, even if there is in them the wrath and anger of its Lord. It does not care, when it wins its desire and portion, whether its Lord is pleased or angered. It is a servant of other than God: in love, fear, hope, pleasure, anger, glorification, and humiliation. If it loves, it loves for its desire; if it hates, it hates for its desire; if it gives, it gives for its desire; if it withholds, it withholds for its desire. Its desire is more preferred by it and more beloved to it than the pleasure of its Master. Desire is its leader, passion its guide, ignorance its driver, and heedlessness its mount. It is immersed in thinking about achieving its worldly aims, and intoxicated with the drunkenness of desire and love of the fleeting. It is called to God and to the Hereafter from a far place, so it does not respond to the adviser, and follows every rebellious devil. The world angers it and pleases it. Desire deafens and blinds it to everything except falsehood. In this world it is like what was said about Layla:

*An enemy to whoever opposes her, and at peace with her people,*
*and whoever Layla brings near, he loves and draws closest.*

So associating with the owner of this heart is sickness, his companionship is poison, and sitting with him is destruction.

**[Section on the diseased heart]**

The third heart is a heart that has life, but with a defect in it. It has two sources of nourishment, one of which supplies it at one time and the other at another time, depending on which prevails over it. In it is what is the source of its life: love of God, faith in Him, sincerity toward Him, and reliance upon Him. And in it is what is the source of its ruin and destruction: love of desires, preference for them, eagerness to obtain them, envy, pride, self-admiration, love of exaltation, and corruption on earth through leadership. It is tested between two callers: one calls it to God, His Messenger, and the Last Day; the other calls it to the fleeting world. It only answers whichever of them is nearer its gate and closer to its neighborhood.

So the first heart is living, humbly submissive, soft, and aware. The second is dry and dead. The third is diseased. It is either closer to safety or closer to destruction.

God, glorified is He, has gathered these three hearts in His words:

﴿We did not send before you any messenger or prophet but that when he desired, Satan cast into his desire. Then God abrogates what Satan casts, then God makes His verses firm, and God is Knowing, Wise.﴾ (22:52)

﴿So that He may make what Satan casts a trial for those in whose hearts is a disease and the hard-hearted, and the wrongdoers are in extreme schism.﴾ (22:53)

﴿And that those given knowledge may know that it is the truth from your Lord, so that they believe in it and their hearts become humbly submissive to it. Indeed God guides those who believe to a straight path.﴾ (22:54)

In these verses God, glorified and exalted is He, made the hearts three: two tested hearts and one saved heart. The two tested ones are the heart in which there is disease and the hard heart. The saved one is the believing heart humbly submissive to its Lord. It is the one at peace with Him, submissive to Him, yielding and obedient.

That is because the heart and the other organs are meant to be sound, without any defect, able to perform what they were made for and created for. Their deviation from uprightness is either through dryness and hardness, and the inability to do what is required of them, like a paralyzed hand, a mute tongue, a flat nose, a man without sexual capacity, or an eye that sees nothing. Or it is through a disease or defect in them that prevents them from perfectly performing these acts and doing them correctly. For this reason the hearts were divided into these three categories.

The sound, healthy heart has nothing between it and accepting the truth, loving it, and preferring it except its perception. It perceives the truth correctly and fully submits to it and accepts it.

The dead, hard heart does not accept it and does not submit to it.

The diseased heart: if its disease prevails over it, it joins the dead, hard heart; and if its soundness prevails over it, it joins the sound heart.

So what Satan casts into the ears as words, and into the hearts as doubts and suspicions, is a trial for these two hearts, and a strength for the living, sound heart. This is because it rejects that, dislikes it, and hates it, knowing that the truth is in its opposite. So its heart humbly submits to the truth, is at peace, and yields. It knows the falsehood of what Satan cast, so its faith in the truth and its love for it increase, and its disbelief in falsehood and its aversion to it increase. So the tested heart is always in doubt about Satan's casting. As for the sound, healthy heart, what Satan casts never harms it at all.

Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said:

"Trials are presented to the hearts like the presenting of a mat, reed by reed. Whatever heart absorbs them, a black spot is marked on it, and whatever heart rejects them, a white spot is marked on it, until hearts become of two kinds: a black heart, dark and inverted like a cup, that recognizes no good and rejects no evil except what has been absorbed from its desire; and a white heart, which no trial harms as long as the heavens and the earth endure."

He likened the presenting of trials to hearts, bit by bit, to the presenting of the reeds of a mat, which are its strands, bit by bit. He divided the hearts, when the trials are presented to them, into two categories:

A heart that is presented with a trial absorbs it, just as a sponge absorbs water, and a black spot is marked on it. It keeps absorbing every trial presented to it until it turns black and becomes inverted. This is the meaning of His words, "like a cup turned upside down" (﴿كالكوز مجخيا﴾), meaning overturned and inverted. When it has blackened and become inverted, two dangerous diseases afflict it, and both lead it to destruction. The first is that the good becomes confused for it with the evil, so it recognizes no good and denounces no evil. This disease may become so entrenched that it considers the good to be evil and the evil to be good, the sunnah (the prophetic way) to be bid'ah (innovation) and the bid'ah to be sunnah, the truth to be falsehood and the falsehood to be truth. The second is that it makes its desire the judge over what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought, and it submits to and follows its desire.

A white heart, in which the light of faith has shone and its lamp has blossomed, rejects and repels any trial presented to it, and its light, radiance and strength increase.

The trials that are presented to hearts are the causes of their sickness. They are trials of desires and trials of doubts, trials of error and misguidance, trials of sins and innovations, and trials of injustice and ignorance. The first kind causes the corruption of intention and will, and the second causes the corruption of knowledge and belief.

The Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, divided hearts into four, as authentically related from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman:
"The hearts are four: a heart that is bare, in which there is a shining lamp, and that is the heart of the believer. A heart that is covered, and that is the heart of the disbeliever. A heart that is inverted, and that is the heart of the hypocrite, who recognizes and then denies, sees and then becomes blind. And a heart that is fed by two streams, the stream of faith and the stream of hypocrisy, and it belongs to whichever of the two prevails over it."

As for his words, "a bare heart," it means one stripped of everything other than Allah and His Messenger. It has been stripped and kept free of everything other than the truth.

"In which there is a shining lamp" refers to the lamp of faith. By its being bare, he indicates its safety from the doubts of falsehood and the desires of error, and by the presence of the lamp in it, he indicates its illumination and brightness with the light of knowledge and faith.

By the covered heart, he refers to the heart of the disbeliever, because it is enclosed within its covering and veil, so the light of knowledge and faith does not reach it, as Allah, the Exalted, said, relating the words of the Jews:
﴿And they say, "Our hearts are covered."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 88]
It is the plural of aghlaf, meaning one enclosed in its covering, like qalaf and aqlaf. This veil is the enclosures (akinnah) that Allah has placed over their hearts as a punishment for them for rejecting the truth and being arrogant toward accepting it. They are enclosures over the hearts, deafness in the ears, and blindness in the eyes. It is the hidden barrier spoken of in His words, the Exalted:
﴿And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a hidden barrier, and We place over their hearts coverings lest they understand it, and in their ears deafness.﴾ [al-Isra': 45-46]
So when the purity of Tawhid (the oneness of Allah) and the purity of following (mutaba'ah, following the Prophet) are mentioned to these hearts, their owners turn their backs in aversion.

By the inverted heart, which is the overturned one, he refers to the heart of the hypocrite, as Allah, the Exalted, said:
﴿Why have you become two groups concerning the hypocrites, while Allah has overturned them for what they earned?﴾ [al-Nisa': 88]
That is, He inverted them and returned them to the falsehood they were in, because of their earning and their false deeds. This is the worst and most wicked of hearts, for it believes falsehood to be truth and allies itself with its adherents, and it considers truth to be falsehood and opposes its people. So Allah is the One sought for help.

By the heart that has two streams, he refers to the heart in which faith has not taken firm root and whose lamp has not blossomed, since it has not been purified for the pure truth with which Allah sent His Messenger. Rather, it contains a portion of that truth and a portion of its opposite. At times it is closer to disbelief than to faith, and at other times closer to faith than to disbelief. The judgment belongs to what prevails, and it is to that that it returns.

As for His words, ﴿that He may make what Satan throws in a trial for those in whose hearts is a disease, and the hard-hearted﴾, the particle here retains its original sense: it is the *lam* of wisdom and causation (*lam al-hikmah wa'l-ta'lil*). God, glorified is He, informs us that He made what Satan had cast into the wish of the Messenger a test and a trial for His servants. Two groups were thereby put to trial: those in whose hearts is a disease, and those whose hearts are hard. He also made the believers know that the Qur'an and the Messenger are true, and that Satan's casting is false. So they believed in this, and their hearts became humbly submissive to it. This is a sought-after and intended end through this divine decree and measure.

God, glorified is He, made hearts into three categories: diseased, hard, and humbly submissive (*mukhbitah*). This is because a heart is either dry and rigid, not softening to the truth in acknowledgment and submission, or it is not like that. The first is the state of hard, stony hearts that do not accept what is instilled in them, in which the truth is not impressed and beneficial knowledge is not engraved, and which do not soften to the performance of righteous deeds. As for the second type, it is either that the truth is firmly established in it and does not depart from it, because of its strength together with its softness, or that it is established with weakness and dissolution. The second is the diseased heart, and the first is the sound, humbly submissive heart. It combines firmness, purity, and softness: it sees the truth through its purity, is strengthened in it through its firmness, and shows mercy to creatures through its softness. As in a transmitted report: "The hearts are the vessels of God on His earth, so the most beloved of them to God are the firmest, the softest and the purest."

As God, the Exalted, said of the people of these hearts: ﴿Hard against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves﴾ (48:29).

This is a description by Him of the believers who recognized faith through the purity of their hearts, were firm against the disbelievers through their hardness, and showed mercy among themselves through their softness. This is because the heart is one of the organs of the body. It is the noblest of its organs and its obeyed sovereign. Every organ, such as the hand for instance, is either rigid and dry, not bending and not gripping, or it grips weakly, and this is like the hard heart. Or it is diseased, weak, and incapable, and due to its weakness and disease, this is like the one who has a disease. Or it is gripping with strength and softness, and this is like the knowing, merciful heart. Through knowledge it has come out of the disease arising from desire and doubt, and through mercy it has come out of hardness. For this reason God, glorified is He, described those other than the owners of the diseased and hard hearts by knowledge, faith, and humble submission. So reflect on the manifestation of His wisdom, glorified is He, in the owners of these hearts, who are the whole community. He informed us that those given knowledge know that it is the truth from their Lord, just as He informed us that they say, regarding the ambiguous (*mutashabih*) verses, "We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord." Both attributes are subject to doubt. So their portion of it was faith, and the portion of the owners of hearts deviating from soundness was trial. For this reason God, glorified is He, made the firm (*ihkam*) rulings of His verses correspond to what Satan casts. The firm verses correspond to the ambiguous ones. So the making firm here is like the sending down of the firm verses there, and the abrogation (*naskh*) of what Satan casts here corresponds to the referral of the ambiguous to the firm there. Abrogation here means lifting what Satan cast, not lifting what the Lord, glorified is He, legislated. Abrogation has another meaning as well: abrogating from the understanding of the addressees what they understood from it that was not intended, and that the wording did not indicate, even if it gave that impression. Just as the Companions applied the term "abrogation" to His words: ﴿Whether you show what is in your souls or conceal it, God will call you to account for it, then He forgives whom He wills﴾ (2:284). They said: "It was abrogated by His words: ﴿Our Lord, do not take us to task if we forget or err﴾ (2:286), and the rest of the verse."

This is abrogation of understanding, not abrogation of an established ruling, since being called to account does not necessarily entail punishment, either in the Hereafter or in this world. For this reason He made the call to account general to them all, then afterwards informed that He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills. So understanding from the verse the taking to task, which is punishment, is loading it beyond its capacity. Therefore this meaning was lifted from their understanding by His words: ﴿Our Lord, do not take us to task if we forget or err﴾, to the end of it.

This is the lifting of an understanding of something other than the intended meaning of what the angel cast, and that is the lifting of what someone other than the angel cast into their hearing or into the wish. Abrogation has a third meaning according to the Companions and the Successors (*tabi'un*): leaving the apparent meaning, either by specifying a general ruling or by restricting an absolute one. This is very frequent in their speech. It has a fourth meaning, which later scholars know and on which they have agreed: lifting a ruling entirely after its establishment by a lifting proof. So these are four meanings of abrogation, and making firm has three meanings.

The first is making firm that corresponds to the ambiguous, as in His words: ﴿He it is who sent down to you the Book, in it are firm verses, which are the mother of the Book, and others ambiguous﴾ (3:7).

The second is making firm that corresponds to the abrogation of what Satan casts, as in His words: ﴿Then God abrogates what Satan casts, then God makes His verses firm﴾ (22:52). This making firm encompasses all His verses: it is their establishment, confirmation, and clarification. Among its uses is His words: ﴿A Book whose verses are made firm﴾ (11:1).

The third is making firm that corresponds to the abrogated verses, as the early generations often say: "This verse is firm and not abrogated." This is because making firm sometimes occurs in the revelation, and then it corresponds to what Satan casts in his wish, whether what the transmitter casts or what enters the transmitter's hearing. The ruling here is what God sent down. God made it firm, that is, He distinguished it from its confusion with what was not sent down, and He separated from it what is not from it by invalidating it. Sometimes it occurs in preserving the revealed text and its continuance, so it is not abrogated after its establishment. And sometimes it occurs in the meaning of the revealed text and its interpretation, which is distinguishing the intended meaning from other meanings so that it is not confused with them.

The point is that His words ﴿so that He may make what Satan casts a trial for those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ have the *lam* of causation in its original sense. This test and trial manifest the three different hearts. The hard and diseased hearts have had their concealed doubt and disbelief exposed. The humbly submissive heart has had its concealed faith and guidance exposed, along with increased love for it and increased hatred of disbelief and polytheism and aversion from them. This is among the greatest wisdoms of this casting.

**[Section: The difference between the angel's inspiration and Satan's casting]**

The difference between the inspiration of the angel and the casting of Satan is in several respects:

Among them: whatever is pleasing to God and in accordance with what His Messenger brought is from the angel, and whatever is for other than Him and not pleasing to Him is from Satan's casting.

Among them: whatever produces turning to God, repentance to Him, remembrance of Him, and an ascending aspiration toward Him is from the angel's casting, and whatever produces the opposite is from Satan's casting.

Among them: whatever produces intimacy, light in the heart, and expansion of the chest is from the angel, and whatever produces the opposite is from Satan.

Among them: whatever produces tranquility and calm is from the angel, and whatever produces anxiety, agitation, and turmoil is from Satan.

The angelic inspiration is frequent in pure, clean hearts that have been illuminated by God's light. The angel has a connection with them and an affinity between him and them, for he is good and pure and only approaches a heart that suits him. So the angel's whisper into this heart is more frequent than Satan's whisper. As for a dark heart that has blackened with the smoke of desires and doubts, Satan's casting and whispering into it are more frequent than the angel's whisper.
